final.title: What transcript accuracy hides in a small business workflow
final.body:
Transcript accuracy can hide the part that actually changes the decision: tone, hesitation, and context. A transcript may be word-perfect and still miss that the customer was unsure, buying time, or quietly objecting. If you run a small business and rely on call notes from sales, support, or onboarding, that gap can change what happens next.

The bounded workflow decision is simple: do you keep treating the transcript as the source of truth, or do you add a check against the original audio or metadata before someone acts on it? I would not force AI into this unless the gap shows up often enough to create rework. Human judgment still belongs in the loop, especially where money or commitments are involved.

A useful diagnostic question is: when we act on a transcript, how often do we later realise we missed hesitation or tone? Don’t guess. Pick 5–10 recent recordings, read the transcript, then listen to the audio beside it and mark every place where the transcript looked clear but the conversation was not.

If that review keeps surfacing the same ambiguity, the next step is not a grand platform project. It is a small pilot to see whether confidence scores, speaker intent, or similar markers would help the team read the conversation more honestly. Tiny truth, less drama.
